title: Artificial Wisdom? A Potential Limit on AI in Law (and Elsewhere)
author: Joshua P. Davis

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The essay does not assess the cluster’s evidence-based account of immediate, bounded workflow gains, verification, training, or competence risks. It instead shifts to a speculative artificial-superintelligence horizon, predicting superiority across technical legal tasks while locating the possible enduring human role in choosing ends and making moral judgments.
qs: And it will be able to describe the law, predict how people will interpret and apply the law, and frame persuasive legal arguments far better than judges and lawyers.
While AI is capable of helping us pursue our ends, it is not clear that AI can choose ultimate ends for us.

st.t: Human oversight: Accountability is not effective control
st.an: The source accepts the importance of retaining substantive human judgment and adds a distinct philosophical basis: AI may lack the first-person perspective, moral agency and conscious deliberation required for some legal decisions. This materially extends the cluster beyond operational oversight and verification, although the argument is explicitly tentative and does not address professional-rule adequacy or empirically demonstrate the claimed limit.
qs: This Essay explores the possibilities that ASI will not be able to conquer the realm of value and that its inability to do so will circumscribe the role it can play in law.
And that distinction may preserve a realm for what human beings are uniquely capable of doing—and what computers may not be capable of doing.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts that AI may perform substantial legal work while humans retain an enduring role, aligning with the cluster’s work-reallocation rather than wholesale-replacement thesis. It materially extends the cluster by identifying moral judgment, subjectivity and moral agency as possible limits on substitution even under artificial superintelligence, while clearly treating that limit as conditional and unproven rather than an established capability barrier.
qs: This Essay suggests three propositions may hold true that would justify an ongoing—perhaps permanent—role for human beings: (1) that moral judgment is necessary for legal and judicial practice; (2) that the first-person perspective (or subjectivity) is necessary for moral judgment; and (3) that AI is incapable of attaining the first-person perspective.
Despite AI’s limitations, it may nonetheless hold the potential to do a great deal of our legal work for us— even if people nevertheless continue to play some role on the bench and in the bar.

st.t: Machine judging: Accuracy cannot establish legitimate authority
st.an: The source supports the proposition that technical capability or accuracy alone cannot justify complete machine adjudication. It argues conditionally that legal judgment sometimes requires moral judgment grounded in subjective experience, while acknowledging extensive AI assistance remains possible. Its contribution is philosophical rather than an institutional account of consent, challenge rights or judicial authority.
qs: It may be that AI is limited to the realm of science, that science cannot fully capture the first-person perspective, that the first-person perspective is necessary to make moral judgments, and that legal and judicial practitioners sometimes must make moral judgments.
If all of that proves true, we may have identified a bulwark against AI taking over all aspects of our legal system.

kp.k: Human legal roles depend on three conditional propositions
kp.d: Davis develops a preliminary philosophical argument, not an empirical finding or demonstrated limit on AI: moral judgment is necessary in legal practice, subjectivity is necessary for moral judgment, and computers cannot achieve subjectivity. If all three hold, humans retain a potentially permanent role in law. The essay briefly considers the first two propositions and concentrates on the third.
qs: First, moral judgments (and other value judgments) are necessary for legal and judicial practice. Second, the subjective perspective is necessary for such judgments. Third, computers (and the material world in which they function) cannot achieve subjective experience.
This Essay does not make a full version of any of those arguments. Its aim is more modest.

kp.k: Superintelligence mastering factual legal tasks is an assumption
kp.d: The essay assumes that artificial superintelligence will surpass humans in factual description, prediction and persuasion, including describing law, anticipating interpretation and framing arguments. Recursive AI improvement and widespread occupational obsolescence are prospective scenarios, not measured legal-market developments; no definite arrival date is supplied.
qs: This Essay proceeds from the assumption that ASI will master the world of fact.
And it will be able to describe the law, predict how people will interpret and apply the law, and frame persuasive legal arguments far better than judges and lawyers.

kp.k: Optimizing means differs from choosing ultimate ends
kp.d: Davis invokes the fact–value distinction and Hume's is–ought problem to suggest that superior factual reasoning need not confer authority or capacity to choose ultimate goals. AI may identify intermediate goals instrumentally once humans supply ultimate ends. The essay assumes that values cannot be reduced to the hard sciences rather than establishing that premise.
qs: While AI is capable of helping us pursue our ends, it is not clear that AI can choose ultimate ends for us.
AI could identify intermediate ends relying solely on ultimate ends provided to it and instrumental reasoning of a factual nature.
This Essay assumes that values cannot be reduced to the hard sciences. But an argument in support of that position is beyond its scope.

kp.k: Major jurisprudential schools preserve moral judgment in practice
kp.d: Davis distinguishes natural law, inclusive positivism and exclusive positivism. They differ over whether morality necessarily, contingently or never determines legal content, but he argues that their major proponents acknowledge moral judgment in legal practice. Even exclusive positivists allow moral reasoning in applying standards or making new law where existing law is indeterminate. Consequently, excluding morality from legal interpretation does not establish that AI could replace all lawyers and judges.
qs: The reason is that there is more to legal or judicial practice than legal interpretation.
The point is that proponents of all of the major jurisprudential schools recognize that morality can play some role in judicial and legal practice.
So if AI is not capable of making moral judgments, it cannot fully perform the role that people play in the law.

kp.k: Dworkin's framework suggests a qualified human–AI division
kp.d: Within Davis's account of Dworkin, AI could assess descriptive fit between legal propositions and authoritative sources, while humans supply normative justification if machines cannot make moral judgments. This is not a clean task separation: choices about interpretive methods themselves involve nested assessments of fit and justification.
qs: They may someday—perhaps someday soon—be better than human beings at assessing fit. But if they cannot make moral judgments, they will not be able to assess justification.
So one must be careful not to exaggerate the ease of disentangling the judgments about fit and justification.

kp.k: Reciprocity offers another constraint on automated legal judgment
kp.d: Davis reports Wendel's ethical argument that legal reason-giving requires mutual accountability among moral agents, and Brennan-Marquez and Henderson's democratic argument for role-reversible judgment. These provide possible reasons to reserve adjudication, and some lawyer functions, for entities capable of being subject to the law themselves. Davis explicitly notes that both arguments assume AI cannot properly be a moral agent and questions whether that might change.
qs: The logic is that those who impose legal judgments on others must themselves be subject to the law.
They contend that it is essential in a democracy that the entity passing judgment under the law could be subject to the law and vice versa.
Note that both of these lines of analysis assume that AI cannot properly be a moral agent.

kp.k: Machine morality remains dependent on human normative inputs
kp.d: Writing in 2019, Davis characterizes AI as unable to select its own ultimate ends. Top-down machine morality requires human-supplied principles; bottom-up approaches require human judgments about desirable actions in examples. A reflective-equilibrium approach would apparently also require preliminary principles, case judgments and rules for reconciling conflicts. He allows that independent operation might follow these inputs, but identifies reasons to doubt its adequacy.
qs: To date, it cannot select its own ultimate ends, moral or otherwise. Human beings must define the goals AI will pursue.

For AI to pursue a reflective equilibrium, human beings would seem to have to provide it at least three forms of guidance: a set of preliminary general principles, a set of intuitions about the right outcomes in particular cases, and a set of rules for reconciling conflicts or tensions between the two.
It is possible that once AI has the necessary inputs from human beings, it could then make moral judgments independently.

kp.k: Novelty, changing values and error require continuing human input
kp.d: Davis proposes three mechanisms sustaining human involvement in AI-mediated legal reasoning: genuinely new circumstances may require novel moral judgments, social moral values may change, and flawed human principles or examples may contaminate machine reasoning. He does not assume changing values necessarily constitute moral progress. Humans may therefore need to update and correct normative inputs rather than merely initialize systems once.
qs: But sometimes new facts require novel moral judgments to place them within existing moral frameworks.
As morality changes, new human input will be necessary for AI to remain accurate in its moral judgments.
Human intervention may be necessary to correct the mistakes embedded in AI ethics by human fallibility.

kp.k: Subjective moral judgment need not imply moral relativism
kp.d: Davis distinguishes needing a first-person perspective to make moral judgments from claiming there are no objectively right or wrong moral answers. He presents non-naturalized objective morality as a conceptual possibility, not a resolved philosophical position. The proposed AI limitation could apply whether moral claims are objectively true or not, provided subjectivity is necessary to assess them.
qs: It is possible that morality may be subjective in the first sense—subjective experience may be necessary to make moral judgments—but not in the second sense—there may be right and wrong answers to (at least some) moral questions.
Of course, to say that something is conceptually possible is not to say that it is true.

kp.k: Scientific explanatory gaps motivate, but do not prove, limits
kp.d: Davis defines the essay's scientific perspective as naturalized materialist reductionism and examines consciousness, free will and the unified self. His argument is that existing scientific accounts do not fully capture first-person experience in ways useful for deliberation, while computers appear explicable within that scientific framework. He expressly leaves open both future machine subjectivity and a future materialist account of subjective experience.
qs: This Essay will treat the scientific perspective as equivalent to a naturalized, materialist reductionism.
To be sure, it may be that computers may someday achieve subjective experience. But, if so, we have no account at present of the conditions that would have to obtain for them to do so.

kp.k: Simulated understanding does not necessarily establish consciousness
kp.d: Davis uses Searle's Chinese Room debate to distinguish manipulating symbols or appearing to understand from actual understanding. He carefully notes that Searle does not rule out future conscious computers. Davis also argues that treating consciousness as an illusion fails to guide first-person deliberation; he does not claim to resolve the philosophy-of-mind debate.
qs: It is important to be clear about Searle’s argument. He does not deny that computers may at some point become conscious. His position instead is that just because a computer can simulate consciousness does not necessarily mean it is conscious.
Accepting that consciousness is not real does not provide guidance for our (apparent) conscious perspective.

kp.k: Scientific insights can improve deliberation without resolving free will
kp.d: Davis contrasts third-person theories of free will with the practical experience of making choices. He reports Kahneman's fast–slow thinking distinction and Libet's wrist-movement experiments, including evidence interpreted as permitting conscious veto of initially unconscious impulses. These illustrate possible improvements to deliberate decision-making, including by lawyers and judges, rather than proof of libertarian free will or established machine incapacity.
qs: But Libet did additional experiments suggesting that while certain—apparently unconscious—brain activity was a necessary predicate for movement, people were able to make a conscious decision later in the process not to move.
None of this necessarily falsifies the claim—by Harris and others—that free will understood in the commonsense libertarian way does not exist.
Third, some insights from science may usefully inform first-person decision-making, but only when they are relatively modest and do not purport to displace free will entirely.

kp.k: Theories of fragmented identity challenge practical first-person reasoning
kp.d: Davis examines controversial modular accounts of the brain and bundle theories denying a persistent self. He argues that these may explain behavior without clearly guiding a deliberating person. Wright's meditation-based response suggests useful distance from impulses but, Davis argues, seems to presuppose a choosing self. Mind-uploading and Parfit's duplication scenarios serve as philosophical thought experiments about identity, not demonstrated technological capabilities.
qs: The modular theory denies the existence of a unified self capable of undergoing experiences, contemplating options, and initiating actions. So what self could act on the knowledge of modularity?

Again, two propositions seem to be true: the third-person, scientific perspective in its pure form seems incompatible with—and unhelpful for—first-person decision-making; and yet some of the insights we gain from science may be helpful to that decision-making, if appropriately adapted.

kp.k: Human judgment does not guarantee protected legal earnings
kp.d: Davis separates preserving a human role from protecting existing legal work or incomes. AI might still perform substantial legal work, increase affordability and access to justice, and intensify competition that makes practice less lucrative. These are conditional possibilities, not measured outcomes. He argues that lawyers' monopoly exists to protect clients rather than attorneys' financial welfare.
qs: Despite AI’s limitations, it may nonetheless hold the potential to do a great deal of our legal work for us— even if people nevertheless continue to play some role on the bench and in the bar.
On one hand, if AI can improve access to legal justice, and make the legal system more affordable, that may well be desirable.
But the monopoly lawyers have on legal practice is meant to protect clients, not the financial well-being of attorneys.

kp.k: Moral roles warrant transparency, not economic complacency
kp.d: Davis encourages judges and lawyers to acknowledge moral and other value judgments in their work. He separately speculates that near-total automation could concentrate gains among machine-owning capital holders and undermine most people's ability to earn a living, requiring radical redistribution. He does not develop an economic policy response; his closing image of moral philosophy as practical vocational preparation illustrates the speculative possibility that normative judgment becomes a remaining human occupation.
qs: It also provides a reason for legal practitioners— judges and lawyers alike—to acknowledge the role that moral and other value judgments play in legal practice.
If the day comes when machines can do almost all of the work we need to do, it is possible that those who control capital—who own the machines—will be able to reap the vast majority of the gains.
Any philosophical limitations on the capacity of AI to engage in legal practice could well prove inadequate to ensure a reasonably just economic order.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Davis assumes that artificial superintelligence could outperform lawyers and judges in factual, predictive, and persuasive legal tasks.
pts.d: The essay's starting scenario is that ASI masters the factual realm, including describing law, predicting its interpretation and application, and framing persuasive arguments. Davis does not present this as a demonstrated legal capability. Even under Dworkin's account of interpretation, he suggests computers could outperform humans at assessing a proposition's fit with authoritative sources, while remaining unable to assess its moral justification.

pts.k: Davis proposes that moral judgment could preserve an ongoing, potentially permanent human role in legal practice despite AI's technical superiority.
pts.d: The proposed limit depends on three propositions: legal practice requires moral judgment; moral judgment requires a first-person perspective; and AI cannot attain that perspective. Davis argues that major jurisprudential schools leave some role for moral judgment in interpretation, application, or making new law. He separately draws on reciprocity arguments to suggest that those imposing legal judgments must themselves be moral agents. This is a conditional philosophical argument, not a finding that AI cannot replace any particular occupation or share of legal work.

pts.k: Davis argues that AI relying on human-supplied morality may need continuing human input to handle novelty, changing values, and errors.
pts.d: Davis distinguishes AI's pursuit of supplied ultimate goals from independently selecting those goals. In top-down and bottom-up approaches to machine morality, humans supply principles or judgments about particular situations. He allows that independent operation after initial input is possible, but suggests changing circumstances, changing moral values, and flawed inputs could require further intervention. In legal practice, this implies humans providing moral reasoning or intuitions when those inform legal decisions, rather than necessarily performing every technical task themselves.

pts.k: Davis suggests AI could perform substantial legal work, improve affordability and access to justice, and intensify competition that reduces lawyers' earnings.
pts.d: The conclusion raises these as possible economic consequences without developing or quantifying them. A continuing human role in morally significant decisions would not prevent extensive automation elsewhere. Davis treats increased affordability and access as potential public benefits, while identifying less lucrative practice as a possible consequence for attorneys.

pts.k: Davis warns that economy-wide automation could concentrate gains with machine owners, regardless of any protected human role in law.
pts.d: In an explicitly speculative extension beyond law, Davis suggests that machines doing almost all necessary work could leave most people with limited ways to earn a living. The resulting distributional problem could require major changes in how economic gains are allocated. His closing example of a student choosing moral philosophy for employment illustrates a possible world in which value judgment remains a human specialty, rather than a concrete career forecast.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The main basis is philosophical argument and cited scholarship, not empirical measurement of AI's legal performance or market effects.
pts.d: For AI's potential, Davis cites chess and Go achievements and literature on recursive improvement and superintelligence, including Kaplan, Good, Bostrom, and Tegmark. For the proposed limit, he reviews natural law and legal positivism, machine-morality approaches, and philosophy-of-mind debates concerning consciousness, free will, and the unified self. He draws on Wendel and Brennan-Marquez and Henderson for reciprocity arguments. Cognitive-science material, including Libet's experiments and Kahneman's account of thinking, informs the discussion of subjectivity; it does not directly test AI's legal or moral judgment. No legal AI benchmark, deployment study, or quantitative legal-market forecast is offered. The economic possibilities are expressly outside the essay's developed argument.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The 2019 essay uses indefinite horizons and explicitly conditions its enduring-human-role thesis on unresolved propositions.
pts.d: Davis describes factual superiority as potentially coming soon and an enduring human role as possibly permanent, but supplies no calendar dates or adoption trajectory. He acknowledges that computers might someday acquire subjective experience and that a scientific account might eventually explain it. His proposed boundary therefore depends on AI remaining unable to make direct moral judgments and on those judgments remaining necessary to legal practice. Even where factual and moral tasks are conceptually distinguishable, he cautions that they may be intertwined in actual interpretation. The economic scenarios are conditional on substantial or near-total automation, not dated forecasts.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims concern lawyers, judges, legal-system users, and, in the broader scenario, workers and capital owners.
pts.d: Lawyers and judges could lose their comparative advantage in description, prediction, and persuasion while retaining responsibility for moral and other value judgments. Attorneys could face stronger competition and lower earnings. Clients and the public could benefit from more affordable legal services and improved access to justice; reciprocity arguments additionally concern people subject to legal judgment. Economy-wide automation could disadvantage workers while benefiting owners of machines. Davis does not distinguish firm sizes, staffing levels, practice-area markets, or provider business models, and does not quantify employment effects.
